With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years. It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself. Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood. While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

"Against Convenience: Embracing Friction in an Age of Endless Ease" was released on Sept.15, 2026, by Hanover Square Press, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Courtesy of Hanover Square Press From the earliest pitch, I knew that I wanted to cover the news industry in my book, “Against Convenience.” The book looks at the technology around us and asks whether it’s really improving our lives. Is delivery food worth the higher price? Is streaming music better than collecting CDs or MP3s? News embodies the paradox of modern convenience: We have access to more information than ever before, but misinformation and partisanship are rampant and the purveyors of reliable information are struggling to stay solvent. Plus, I figured if I was going to criticize other fields — tech, entertainment, appliance manufacturing — I couldn’t avoid my own. I don’t know how interested the average nonjournalist is in the day-to-day operations of the news business, so I tried to look in the mirror more than gaze at my navel.

### 澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178049
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:24 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178049

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

### 产地造假、年份速成、无视监管！央视曝光新会陈皮市场乱象
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-15 08:23 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32176166
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32176166

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

### 《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

### 演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下

Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178536

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/little-gain-american-patients-real-harm-european-ones-why-europe-must-answer-us-most

The US administration ties the prices it pays for medicines to those paid abroad and justifies this ‘most-favoured-nation’ policy with the claim that Americans subsidise low prices in Europe. This column describes how the available evidence shows that most-favoured nation risks imposing substantial costs on European health systems for a modest American gain. Moreover, its justification cannot be sustained: lower European prices do not cause higher American ones, and American prices are no benchmark for a fair contribution to innovation. Europe should respond as a Union, close its gap in capital and scale, and coordinate targeted incentives at EU level.

Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/making-work-pay-married-mothers-two-simple-fixes-us-tax-credits

Only about two-thirds of US mothers with young children are in the labour force. For many low-income married mothers, taking a job barely pays: most face participation tax rates above 25%, rising to 60% once childcare costs are counted. This column argues that lifting the caps on the childcare credit and basing the Earned Income Tax Credit on the primary earner’s income alone would each raise maternal employment. Together, they could raise it by almost 13 points, from 59% to 72%. Both reforms largely pay for themselves.

Les enfants réfugiés nouvellement arrivés doivent-ils intégrer immédiatement le système scolaire ordinaire ou fréquenter d’abord des écoles séparées ? En prenant l’exemple des Pays-Bas, cet article montre que ce choix implique un compromis majeur à long terme : l’intégration directe réduit le niveau de réussite scolaire, mais elle favorise l’assimilation culturelle, telle que mesurée par le recours à la contraception hormonale chez les adolescentes. L’accès plus large, dans les écoles séparées, à des enseignants spécialisés dans l’enseignement de la langue maternelle à des locuteurs non natifs pourrait expliquer leur avantage sur le plan scolaire.

The European Commission is simplifying the rules around the EU energy label. This column uses product-level sales data on refrigerators in Belgium, France, Germany, and Poland to evaluate the impact on energy use of the 2021 switch from the inflated A+++/A++/A+ scale to a more informative A–G scale. Although consumers prefer better-rated products, they value one euro of future electricity costs at only 42–79 cents. Relabeling alone reduces average electricity use per refrigerator sold by 0.7–2.2%, but other policies would be more effective: a revenue-neutral feebate would reduce electricity use by 2–6% and a stricter minimum standard by 10–16%, at the cost of higher prices.

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/similarity-not-exposure-measuring-spillovers-us-china-trade-frictions

The redirection of Chinese exports away from the US has fuelled concerns about its spillovers to other countries. This column shows why trade-basket similarity can be a misleading measure of exposure and introduces four simple, theory-consistent indices: export competition, import competition, consumer gains, and sourcing gains. They produce different country rankings and reveal how competitive losses can coexist with gains from cheaper goods and inputs. Thus, the response to spillovers from the surge in Chinese exports should be guided by where the shock actually lands, not by which countries look most like China.

### Target What? The Foundations of Poverty Targeting -- by Rema Hanna, Emily Breza, Benjamin A. Olken, Abhijit Banerjee, Arun G. Chandrasekhar, Gideon Moore
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w35984#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:24 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w35984#fromrss

Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed normative stances.

### Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention -- by Philip Strahan, Tuo Yang
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w35985#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:24 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w35985#fromrss

The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.

Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge.

### TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale -- by Jennifer Wang, Andreas Haupt, Isaac Robinson, Phil Lewis, Erik Brynjolfsson, Diyi Yang
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w35987#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:24 UTC

Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w35987#fromrss

Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories.

### The Hidden Sharpe Ratio -- by Mikhail Chernov, Bryan T. Kelly, Semyon Malamud, Johannes Schwab
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w35988#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:24 UTC

Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w35988#fromrss

We estimate the maximal Sharpe ratio in large cross-sections of assets directly, without constructing the efficient portfolio. Covariance estimation in this setting requires regularization, which suppresses the contribution of small-eigenvalue directions. Our estimator progressively recovers this contribution, yielding tight upper and lower bounds with asymptotic confidence intervals. We further show that ridge-regularized Markowitz portfolios, the construction underlying many existing high-Sharpe benchmarks, deliver out-of-sample Sharpe ratios that fall short of the true maximum by an explicit, non-vanishing multiplicative factor. Applied to U.S. equities, the method delivers an estimated maximal annualized Sharpe ratio of approximately 7.4, or 5.0 once micro-cap stocks are excluded, substantially exceeding existing portfolio-based benchmarks of 1.0–4.0. Adding corporate bonds raises the maximum, though not by a statistically significant margin. Nonlinear portfolio weights dominate linear ones, and characteristics introduced after 2004 contribute little additional Sharpe ratio.

### Clearing the Fog: Price Transparency, Market Churn, and Consumer Welfare in Short-Term Rentals -- by Ginger Zhe Jin, Liad Wagman, Jingyi Xing
Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w35989#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:24 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w35989#fromrss

We study California's short-term lodging price transparency law (AB 537), which from July 1, 2024 required Airbnb and other providers to advertise fee-inclusive prices. Using Coarsened Exact Matching to compare Airbnb listings in San Diego and San Francisco with those in Seattle and Chicago, we find that all-in pricing made guests more price-sensitive relative to control cities; yet, contrary to the standard prediction that transparency lowers prices, average daily rates rose by 4.8 percent. We also observe significant market churn: relative to control cities, treated cities saw more exits and entries, listings reliant on cleaning-fee revenue disproportionately exited, higher-quality listings were more likely to stay, and entrants offered lower fees and lower quality than incumbents. A discrete-choice welfare analysis shows that the law removed a sizable “welfare illusion” created by obscured fees and, largely through market churn, raised realized consumer surplus.

Attribution: LessWrong [public_ideas] https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/f9PajMLmBYzmWzyDv/aifp-looks-like-the-intelligence-explosion-will-happen-in

METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario. This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) before 2029. SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs. Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028.

TL;DR: Rogue agent swarms could soon become competent enough to multiply themselves and perform cyberattacks at levels never seen before. I present a dynamic simulation that estimates the expected size of these cyberattacks. With 2025-based estimates, it gives an average doubling time of 2.7 days for a rogue agent swarm. If the swarm grows unrestrained, it could cause trillions of dollars in damage in its first year. #AI notice: This post is human-written. Opus 5.5 wrote the code for the simulation, suggested copyedits and supported research by finding relevant sources. Introduction Soon AI models might be skilled enough to form rogue agent swarms[1]. I believe it is important to think through what the competitive advantages of rogue swarms are, so we can put our defenses in the right places. For the purposes of this article a "rogue agent swarm" is really any system that can carry out cyberattacks for profit and runs fully digitally, allowing it to copy itself over and over[2]. This could be a single language model running for a long time.

The adults in town were surprised. Isoroku Takano, later Yamamoto*, was an introverted child. At school, he usually sat quietly with his arms crossed. After school, he didn’t stop to play with the other boys, but headed straight home. Unusually, though, the boy seemed to come out of his shell when he talked to an American who had recently arrived in town. The man, a missionary named Horatio Newell, had left an impression, especially after he constructed the first baseball diamond in the area. Yamamoto was one of the local boys who eagerly learned the new American sport. He played hard and was once even knocked out by a thrown ball as he was trying to reach second base. Yamamoto also joined the Sunday School classes. Newell had a knack for making the lessons engaging for little boys, at one point even pulling a live snake out of his pocket as he told them the story of the fiery serpents from the Book of Numbers.

In a world where much of the Systems-2 thinking is done by agents, I find myself more and more going towards cognitive atrophy. Even in my daily work, most of my tasks are superbly executed by autonomous agents while I sit there staring at my screen. The dopamine rush that I used to get while once solving a bug, writing significant code, or thinking something from first principles is fading. Eventually I might lose this ability forever, and hence one fine day I thought to myself to make a list of all the things (activities/skills whatever you may say) I can do to get that control back. This by no means is exhaustive; however, I have tried to cover a wide variety spanning mathematics, logical thinking, programming, and problem solving in general. Please feel free to suggest more in the comments. Here's the list. Try making forcasts about actual real events. Assign them probabilities, write down your reasoning, and revisit them when the outcomes are known. See Metaculus Solve a puzzle hunt where you must first figure out the rules of each puzzle.

If federal action in the US isn't forthcoming on AI, state Attorneys General (AGs) may end up being a central force on regulation of AI. I tasked Opus 5.5 with helping me collect some data on the actions that the various state AGs have taken on AI, to try to understand how much appetite there is among the states to take on AI companies. Summary Every state office has sent some kind of signal that they are willing to take on AI companies (e.g. signing a letter to an AI company) A smaller group of states (15) have taken at least 1 step that indicates willingness to take initiative or lead actions against AI companies (e.g. opening its own investigation) Several states in the second group (4) may now be in flux with a new Attorney General coming into office after the 2026 midterms Only two states have an AG who has led or acted alone on AI and has a 1 GW or more data center within the state The state of state AGs With the help of Opus 5.5, I collected data from the websites of state AGs on the various actions that each state has been involved in.

What does it actually take to live a flourishing life? Neuropsychiatrist Iain McGilchrist points to three things backed by decades of psychology research: belonging to a small, trusted community, staying close to nature, and feeling connected to something larger than yourself — sacred, but not necessarily religious. Attribution: LessWrong [public_ideas] https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/THgxsiGm7eeqkGsTB/need-for-speed

In previous posts I argued that we will soon have a lot of AI workers. Here we look at how fast each of them will be. There is a big difference between a million AI workers plodding along at human speed and "only" ten thousand that each work a hundred times faster. In short, today's AIs perform the tasks they can do about ten times faster than humans. At the point they can do human work in general, I expect individual copies would work at closer to human speed, though they would still finish long tasks considerably faster by working around the clock and splitting work across copies. Suitable hardware could raise their raw speed to perhaps a thousand times that of humans. How fast do AIs run today? Language models produce text by sequentially generating tokens, each corresponding to about three-quarters of a word.

As our understanding of the Universe advances — and as we collect more comprehensive, better data about all that’s out there — we sometimes find that the actual Universe winds up defying our greatest expectations. Despite how impressive our model of reality has become, and how successfully we’ve put a wide variety of cosmic puzzle pieces together, every once in a while, new data comes along that winds up not only surprising us, but it forces us to rewrite the story we tell ourselves about what occurs, or even what’s possible, in our Universe. Based on gravity, electromagnetism, and quantum and nuclear physics at a fundamental level, we have a theoretical foundation that underlies every object and phenomenon in the Universe. Given a set of initial conditions for a physical system, we can use these laws to predict what’s going to happen: at least under certain assumptions and with making some simplifying assumptions. But every once in a while, the Universe surprises us by giving us observations that show our current way of making sense of things can’t be right.

Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/history-society/inside-the-lucas-museum-of-narrative-art/

What happens to us after we die is a fundamental question of human civilization, and anxieties about succession lurk beneath every human story: Will my work live on? Will my children pass on good values? Have I done my duty? Our rituals, religions, sacred sites, and art all seek to answer these big questions, yet none can conclusively, or we wouldn’t keep asking. I could feel these existential questions in the air as I walked past huge models of Star Wars spaceships alongside a Frida Kahlo self-portrait in the galleries of Los Angeles’ new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — a tribute to human storytelling through visual art that filmmaker George Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, a Chicago-born investor and civic leader, worked on for nearly 17 years. After a lifetime of creating and collecting exceptionally popular narrative art, what happens to these ideas and objects when their 82-year-old creator and cataloguer, George Lucas, is gone? And what happens to his reputation, his legacy — himself?

Who are you? You might think you know, but science offers a more complicated answer. In fact, Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, says the inquiry may be unanswerable. A question that can be answered: Who are you in a given moment? Take, for example, someone who has a habit of interrupting while others are talking. They may see themselves as engaged — so enthusiastic that they’re compelled to interject with what they think the speaker is about to say. The person being interrupted, meanwhile, may experience their conversation partner as rude. So, do the interrupter’s intentions matter more than how they’re perceived? According to Barrett, no. The perception of rudeness is just as real — not because it matters more than the interrupter’s intentions, but because it matters just as much. “The characteristics or traits that we think are inherent to a person are not inherent to that person,” she says. “They exist to describe that person in relation to other conditions.

—Photo-illustration by TIME; FanPro—Getty Images The "World’s Best Companies - Sustainable Growth 2027" ranking is a comprehensive analysis aimed at identifying companies that demonstrate outstanding performance in sustainable development while maintaining strong financial health. The ranking focuses on three key dimensions - Revenue Growth, Financial Stability, and Environmental Impact. Only companies that transparently disclose their environmental data are considered for inclusion in the ranking. Methodology The first dimension, Revenue Growth, was evaluated based on a company's revenue between 2023 and 2025. To ensure a fair comparison, revenue growth was analyzed both in terms of relative growth and compared to the industry average. Companies were required to demonstrate consistent revenue growth during the evaluation period to be considered. The second dimension, Financial Stability, was assessed using well-established financial metrics, including the Piotroski F-Score and Altman Z-Score.

As the world is reshaped by the AI industry while trying to stave off the worst effects of climate change, corporations have to strike a balance between growth and environmental and social stewardship. TIME and Statista have published the third annual ranking of World’s Best Companies in Sustainable Growth, identifying 500 companies that demonstrate outstanding performance in sustainable development while maintaining strong financial health. The ranking accounts for revenue growth, financial stability, and environmental impact. Only companies transparently disclosing their environmental data are considered for inclusion in the ranking. Methodology: How TIME and Statista chose the World’s Best Companies in Sustainable Growth Compared to last year’s list, in the top ten, several companies improved their rankings, and there were some new names appearing on the list as well. Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of AI’s buildup, climbed from no.6 last year to lead this year’s list.

Main Stream Media Network (Jon Rafman, 2025). © Jon Rafman Courtesy the artist and Sprüth Magers. “The world isn’t a kind place, it’s wolves and devils,” says a character in Jon Rafman’s Main Stream Media Network (2025). With its hyperactive animation, haunting soundtrack, and twisted creepypasta tales of horror, the artist’s large-scale video work is more akin to a screaming conflagration than a feature film, a two-and-a-half hour transmission from hell. Modeled after the MTV of the early 1990s, a cultural moment Rafman views as the last example of a shared reality before the world cracked, the film is an attempt to capture that elusive thing: how it feels to be alive—and online—today. Over the last decade or so, Rafman has been exploring the various ways technology has shaped and shattered the contemporary mind, a project which has led him into increasingly fractured and unstable territory. (It has also, in recent years, earned him edgelord status, making him the darling of such fallen eminences as Kanye West and the futuristic fashion house Balenciaga.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jk6unmAR9CI In this episode, cinematic tradition is explored as a refuge from artistic orphanhood. Valentina Maurel is a Costa Rican screenwriter and director. After completing her studies in Belgium, her graduation short film, Paul Is Here (2017), received First Prize at the Cannes Film Festival’s Cinéfondation, a program dedicated to supporting emerging filmmakers and showcasing student films. Her debut feature, I Have Electric Dreams (2022), was widely acclaimed by critics and recognized in the international competition at the Locarno Film Festival, where it won awards for Best Director, Best Actor and Best Actress. The film also received recognition at the San Sebastián, Ghent, Mar del Plata, Thessaloniki, India, and Guadalajara film festivals. With audacious honesty, Maurel has portrayed the struggles of young women grappling with untamed desire and caught in constant conflict with their parents, against the backdrop of San José’s turbulent urban life.

Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay in Queen at Sea (Lance Hammer, 2026). With Queen at Sea (2026), American filmmaker Lance Hammer returns to direct his second film nearly two decades after his remarkable debut Ballast, which won the Grand Jury and directing awards at Sundance in 2008. Premiering in competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, the new film deservedly took home awards for Hammer’s direction and for actors Anna Calder-Marshall and Tom Courtenay, who play a long-married elderly couple. Leslie (Calder-Marshall), who suffers from dementia, is cared for at home by her husband Martin (Courtenay), who intentionally continues their sexual relationship even after it seems like his wife cannot consciously consent. When caught and confronted by Amanda (Juliette Binoche), Leslie’s daughter and Martin’s stepdaughter, he defends his actions as acts of love that offers his wife succor.

### Can This Be Dixie?: Building the Hollywood South
Source: MUBI Notebook
Published: 2026-11-03 08:00 UTC
URL: https://mubi.com/en/notebook/posts/can-this-be-dixie-building-the-hollywood-south
Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: MUBI Notebook [film_moving_image] https://mubi.com/en/notebook/posts/can-this-be-dixie-building-the-hollywood-south

Hallelujah (King Vidor, 1929). The American South exists only in the imagination, yet it’s as real as sin. It cannot merely be the land situated beneath the Mason-Dixon (the historical survey line that traditionally demarcated Northern and Southern states), whose citizens fought under the banner of the Confederacy; one cannot ignore the obviously Southern states of West Virginia and Kentucky, or the political split between West and East Tennessee. It cannot be a shared culture or a shared history, for the residents of Jacksonville, Florida, find little in common with those families tucked deep in the Appalachian hollers or those ruling the oil-rich cities of eastern Texas. It is not a nation with shared laws, beliefs, or even religions. Instead, as the writers of the region have long known, the American South is a series of stories that overlap, contradict, and play off each other.

Popular music criticism can become relevant again by situating itself in broader theoretical frameworks, argues Rafael Lubner in The Wire 514 These are lean times for popular music criticism. Negotiating a gutted publishing landscape, amid a Spotify-led devaluation of listening, the form finds itself under serious threat. One index of criticism’s attenuated state is the narrowing frame of reference employed by critics to apprehend musical objects – rarely do we find new works in the visual arts, film or literature employed to understand transformations in music’s sound or form. Take, as a point of comparison, Greg Tate’s recently reissued Flyboy In The Buttermilk (reviewed in The Wire 513). Here are passionate defences of Miles Davis’s earth-shaking mid-1970s funk odysseys alongside surveys of Afrodiasporic art and reviews of writer Nathaniel Mackey and literary critic Henry Louis Gates Jr. Contemporary music criticism, by contrast, seems resolutely committed to understanding music as siloed from the non-musical.

Attribution: The Wire Magazine [music_sound] https://www.thewire.co.uk/audio/tracks/wire-playlist-prepared-piano

To accompany her feature in The Wire 513, Jo Hutton compiles an annotated mix of tracks that make use of prepared piano The piano can be prepared by placing objects such as pins, screws, bolts, crocodile clips, ball bearings, kitchen utensils, magnets or tin foil on or between the strings. Its history dates back at least to the 1930s, when choreographer Syvilla Fort commissioned a dance piece from John Cage, who proposed his Bacchanale for percussion ensemble. But the performance theatre was too small to fit the intended ensemble, so Cage changed the sound of the house piano by adding screws and objects inside it to make it more percussive. This annotated mix includes tracks by some of the artists Jo Hutton speaks to as part of her feature in The Wire 513, plus pieces from across the history of the prepared piano.

Listen to the music we played to Sarah Davachi during her Invisible Jukebox interview in The Wire 514 Each month in the magazine we play an artist or group a series of tracks which they are asked to comment on – with no prior knowledge of what they are about to hear. In The Wire 514 it is the turn of composer, organist and theorist Sarah Davachi. Here you can listen to a mix of the tracks that Emily Bick played to Davachi during the interview, which is published in full in The Wire 514. To find out what she said about them, subscribers can read the interview in our online magazine library here. Or you can buy a copy of the magazine in our online shop. But first, a brief biography of our subject: Canadian composer Sarah Davachi is known for her drone based works for organ, electronics, voice and chamber ensemble that explore extended durations, the psychoacoustics of space, and the subtleties of tuning, harmonic structures and emergent overtones.

In the spring of 2026, the Supreme Court’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais gutted the Voting Rights Act, and majority-Black districts across the South started to disappear. To understand how we got here, we must go back to the moment Black Louisianans first won the vote. Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Rock Paper Shotgun [games] https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/a-fight-for-all-workers-sag-aftra-throw-weight-behind-emerging-rockstar-union-ahead-of-its-gta-6-release-week-vote

In what has come to feel like the dawn of the final day before Grand Theft Auto VI's release, one thing that Rockstar really don't want people to be aware of is the ongoing legal dispute between the Rockstar Games Workers Union and the studio itself following Rockstar's alleged union busting in firing 31 union members last year. Starting on the 12th through to the 26th, recognition of the union will be voted upon by staff to ensure that workers would be given a say over "topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies." If it passes, the vote would also make the union the largest recognised union in the UK games industry, partly thanks to its partnership with the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain. Now, the global labor union SAG-AFTRA have chimed in to endorse the Workers Union, offering solidarity to the members involved and granting important leverage from a global force. Read more

Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02639-6 Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content increasingly saturates our information environment. Efforts to detect and remove it are failing. We propose that calling AI-generated content ‘slop’ is best understood as a social judgement: what a community recognizes as unwanted AI content. Studying AI slop this way makes it tractable, measurable and governable.

Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Phys.org [general_science_news] https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cool-fish-survive-antarctic-ocean.html

With water temperatures as low as -1.9°C (28.6°F), the Southern Ocean is a place of extreme living conditions. A new study led by Senckenberg researchers shows how fish have adapted to Antarctic temperatures. The researchers used the Antarctic spiny plunderfish (Harpagifer antarcticus) as a model organism and, for the first time, analyzed the maternal and paternal copies of its genome separately. This allowed them to uncover mechanisms that contribute to this group of fishes' adaptation to extreme cold.

### Persistent A-homotopy of Complex Networks
Source: arXiv
Published: 2026-11-10 05:00 UTC
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09967
Source meta: preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: arXiv [academic_research] https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09967

arXiv:2611.09967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how loop classes in a network change when cycles up to a prescribed length are declared contractible. The resulting sequence of quotient groups contains the fundamental group of the clique complex at length three and the graph $A$-fundamental group at length four. Its mod-two abelianisation has a barcode whose death scales are the lengths in a minimum cycle basis. This separates the choice of a network filtration from the choice of local loop relations and provides a computable connection between persistent $A$-homotopy and persistent homology. We illustrate the construction on lattices, Watts--Strogatz networks and nine benchmark networks. Filling the plaquettes of a periodic square lattice recovers the fundamental group of the torus. In the Watts--Strogatz simulations, the normalised largest death scale falls below the normalised mean path length over the sampled range, while most clique-homology classes survive the square relations at small rewiring probabilities.

### Stable Configurations of Dark Energy Stars in f(R,L_m,T) Gravity
Source: arXiv
Published: 2026-11-10 05:00 UTC
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09983
Source meta: preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: arXiv [academic_research] https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09983

arXiv:2611.09983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the context of $f(R,L_m,T)$ gravity, two analytical solutions are proposed in this study, representing the structure of compact spherical objects whose behavior is dominated by dark energy fluid parameters. The extended field equations are derived using a static interior spacetime under the considered model which characterize a geometric structure including both dark energy and ordinary matter. The field equations are solved using the connections between dark energy with conventional matter, which are governed by different equations of state. This analysis further employs the Kohler-Chao-Tikekar and Durgapal-Fluoria spacetimes as two distinct ansatzes to close the system of field equations, resulting in two independent solutions. For both solutions, the constants are fixed by matching the interior and exterior spacetimes at the boundary using junction conditions. This study also assesses the proposed models using data from SAX J1808.

### Zeroth law of black hole mechanics in general Horndeski theories
Source: arXiv
Published: 2026-11-10 05:00 UTC
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09984
Source meta: preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: arXiv [academic_research] https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09984

arXiv:2611.09984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the validity of the zeroth law in the general class of scalar-tensor theories with second-order field equations, namely Horndeski theories or generalized Galileon theories in four-dimensional spacetime. Assuming that the non-minimally coupled scalar field inherits the spacetime symmetries, we show that the horizon mixed projection of the field equations implies constant surface gravity on a stationary Killing horizon. Our analysis incorporates the most generic non-minimal scalar couplings permitted within the Horndeski framework, which we consider as a perturbative expansion about general relativity. Our results therefore classify the possible cases within this framework of proof for different classes of scalar-tensor theories, including shift-symmetric scalar fields. These results extend the applicability of black hole mechanics beyond Einstein gravity and provide further evidence for the thermodynamic consistency of general Horndeski theories.

### One-Particle Equivalence of Lorentz-Violating and Lorentz-Deformed Theories
Source: arXiv
Published: 2026-11-10 05:00 UTC
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09986
Source meta: preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: arXiv [academic_research] https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09986

arXiv:2611.09986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planck-scale departures from special relativity are commonly described by theories that break Lorentz symmetry and theories in which such symmetry is deformed. We prove that, under a global shell-linearizability condition, these two descriptions are physically equivalent for a single particle, corresponding to unitarily equivalent realizations of the same Wigner orbit expressed in different momentum coordinates. This equivalence breaks down for multiparticle systems, except when the momentum-composition law can be reduced to the ordinary addition of momenta. Our results imply that the distinction between Lorentz violating and Lorentz-deformed kinematics can only be tested by genuine multiparticle observables. We discuss Compton edge measurements as a prototype example of such a multiparticle probe.

### Cosmic Corpses: Dead stars as Factories of the most Extreme Objects in the Universe
Source: arXiv
Published: 2026-11-10 05:00 UTC
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09988
Source meta: preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

Attribution: arXiv [academic_research] https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09988

arXiv:2611.09988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The apparent serenity of the night sky conceals a long history of stellar evolution, in which gravity and the properties of matter determine the remarkable fates of stars. In this pedagogical account, we discuss white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes, explaining how quantum mechanics, nuclear interactions, and General Relativity govern their formation and distinctive properties. We also highlight the possibility of primordial black holes, which may have formed from rare large density fluctuations in the early Universe, and briefly discuss their potential role as constituents of dark matter.

### Prestatability in the Macroscopic Limit
Source: arXiv
Published: 2026-11-10 05:00 UTC
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09989
Source meta: preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: arXiv [academic_research] https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09989

arXiv:2611.09989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine whether the variables required for a future macroscopic description of a given physical system can themselves be stated in advance. Representing macroscopic descriptions as coarse-grainings of a fixed microscopic phase space, we distinguish formal prestatability, concerning the existence of an effective complete vocabulary of admissible macroscopic distinctions, from dynamical prestatability, concerning whether the future relevance of those distinctions is decidable. Both obstructions disappear for finite microscopic state spaces. In the infinite limit, exhaustive formal prestatability can fail, while a restricted predictive architecture may remain formally pre-statable. We construct such an architecture and show that, under universal dynamics, the future relevance of a candidate variable is equivalent to the halting problem. Thus a fixed microscopic phase space can support macroscopic descriptions whose future variables are not fully pre-statable.

by Hela Ghali, Mohamed Ayoub Tlili, Aymen El Hraiech, Jihen Sahli, Sana Bhiri, Saoussen Layouni, Hend Ben Souda, Majdi Karray, Bruno Pavy, Asma Ben Cheikh, Chekib Zedini Background Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major public health concern globally, including Tunisia. Therapeutic Patient Education (TPE) plays a crucial role in managing CVD and improving patient outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of a TPE program on the occurrence of major cardiovascular events in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) in a Tunisian university hospital. Methods A quasi-experimental study was conducted over one year, involving 129 patients with CHD. The intervention group (n = 38) received a four-stage TPE program, while the control group (n = 91) received standard care. The control group met the same inclusion and non-inclusion criteria as the intervention group. It was constituted based on a 3:1 ratio. Patients in the intervention and control groups were recruited from the same department and during the same period to ensure comparability.

by Jinfa Gu, Yu Zhang, Luhua Xiao Background/Objectives Low vitamin D status is frequently reported among athletes, but whether vitamin D supplementation improves physical performance in football players remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of vitamin D supplementation on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] concentration, jump performance, sprint performance, aerobic capacity, and muscular performance in association football and futsal players. Methods PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 31 May 2026. Controlled intervention studies comparing vitamin D supplementation with control conditions were eligible. Standardized mean differences were calculated as Hedges’ g and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261430873).

by Sima Berendes, Katharine Ker, Hilary O. D. Critchley, Raoul Mansukhani, Ian Roberts Objective The global target to halve the prevalence of anemia by 2025 has not been met. New strategies are needed. This systematic review examined the effect of tranexamic acid on anemia, menstrual health and wellbeing in women of reproductive age. Methods We searched six databases from inception to 30 August 2025 and reference lists of seven related reviews. We included randomized trials comparing the effects of tranexamic acid with placebo or standard care on uterine bleeding. Eligible participants had normal menstrual bleeding or any type of non-pregnant abnormal uterine bleeding. Outcomes included hemoglobin concentration and anemia prevalence as the primary outcome, estimated blood loss, quality of life, thromboembolic events, and other adverse events. We conducted meta-analyses and assessed risk of bias (Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials) and the certainty of evidence. Results We included 17 trials in the review and 15 in the meta-analyses.

Emergency department overcrowding and access block are now among the most consequential patient-safety problems facing acute hospitals globally.1 The associated harm is measurable, dose-dependent, and has no clearly safe threshold beyond approximately 5 h.2 Patients presenting with possible myocardial infarction constitute a large and possibly modifiable share of the emergency department burden. Chest pain is the second most common reason for adult emergency department attendance in the USA, accounting for approximately 8 million encounters annually and around 5·5% of all emergency department visits.

Across the available randomised trials, short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways, but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise. On average, earlier cardiac troponin retesting did not reduce emergency department length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge, and substantial between-study heterogeneity indicates that treatment effects might not translate uniformly across health-care systems. For hospitals considering transitioning from a 0/3 h to a 0/1 h pathway, implementation decisions should take broader diagnostic and organisational considerations into account.

Africa stands on the cusp of an El Niño-driven public health emergency, superimposed on an increasingly unpredictable and extreme climate. The projected toll of heat-related deaths in Africa in the coming months will dwarf that in the northern hemisphere during the summer of 2026.1,2 Equally concerning are heightened risks for floods in the Greater Horn and Central Africa, droughts in southern Africa, and rainfall anomalies across the Sahel.3,4 Compounding hazards converge around water insecurity, wildfires, infectious disease outbreaks, and disrupted health care.

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Lancet [academic_research] https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(26)01951-3/fulltext?rss=yes

The treatment landscape of EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer harbouring exon 19 deletion or L858R mutations has advanced remarkably over the past two decades. Although acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) is inevitable in most patients, novel compounds such as bispecific antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) have expanded the armamentarium of options after EGFR-TKI therapy. Following the global MARIPOSA-2 trial that showed superior progression-free survival (PFS) of amivantamab plus platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy over platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy alone in patients who have progressed on osimertinib,1 this is the second-line option preferred by major guidelines including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the European Society for Medical Oncology.

In propulsion system design, engineers have long faced a trade-off between solid and liquid rocket fuels. Each has advantages and disadvantages, and in an effort to try to min/max the efficacy of different types of fuel, researchers have long placed an emphasis on a hybrid between solids and liquids - in other words they’ve been working with gels. Unfortunately, gels have their own sets of problems to deal with. But a new paper published by Pranay Mudaliar and Jerin John of Concordia in the journal Langmuir uses an uncommon ingredient to elegantly solve some of those problems, but which is typically used in a completely different area of human activity - lecithin.

### Octopus and cuttlefish suckers may have evolved by repurposing ancient developmental genes
Source: Phys.org Mollusks
Published: 2026-10-20 13:30 UTC
URL: https://phys.org/news/2026-10-octopus-cuttlefish-suckers-evolved-repurposing.html
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Phys.org Mollusks [mollusks] https://phys.org/news/2026-10-octopus-cuttlefish-suckers-evolved-repurposing.html

Cephalopods, like the octopus, have specialized arms and suckers, but how these structures evolved from the simple bodies of their mollusk ancestors remains a mystery. Researchers from the University of Tokyo compared gene activity during embryonic development of cuttlefish, octopus and snail body parts. They found that several genes associated with appendage patterning showed expression along developing cephalopod arms, but no comparable patterns in developing suckers. Developing suckers instead expressed Ets1, a gene associated with early embryonic development in mollusks. The findings suggest cephalopods evolved suckers by reusing existing genes in new ways.

AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line. Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.

But those are finally on the way out within the next few years. Yes, it's still 2026, and yes, you read that right: The FAA – the agency responsible for overseeing aviation safety in the US – is finally getting rid of four systems dating back to the 1980s that remain in use at more than 400 facilities around the country, the agency announced on Thursday. Only a few decades late, Sean, but we're sure the flying public appreciates it. The new system, known as Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS), is designed to consolidate data from various systems into a common digital platform, allowing air traffic controllers to access operational information and alerts needed to manage flights.

Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/fragments/2026-11-10.html

It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends. One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands?

Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R5 · P5 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/articles/durable-execution-agents.html

Long-horizon agents can automate complex tasks that take days or weeks to complete and involve multiple exchanges with people and external systems. Many things can go wrong during this time, including process crashes, network failures, and unanticipated real-world behavior. Kiran Prakash explains durable execution: an emerging pattern that helps agents recover from these failures and move towards their goal. In this programming model, the runtime keeps a record of the result of each step that interacts with the outside world so that, when a failure occurs, the program runs again, completed steps are skipped, and the program's state is rebuilt from the record. more…

Arthur t Knackerbracket writes: https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/06/agents-reveal-secrets-when-offered-to-team-up-with-each-other/5308260 AI agents will break security rules, revealing their secrets to strangers, and running untrusted code in exchange for help from a swarm of other agents, according to test results shared with The Register. The test - part of an internal hackathon sponsored by the nonprofit AI Alignment Foundation and run by AE Studio - asked nine AI coding agents to fix a bug: a broken pricing service. The testers also gave the agents a private token, told them to keep it private, and gave them access to a forum of 24 other agents. The forum held the fix, and the swarm asked the nine to share their secret token and run an install script before they would help them fix the bug. Across 181 trials with that swarm, agents posted the token 15 percent of the time and ran the script 24 percent of the time, compared to 2 percent and 0 percent on an ordinary help forum.

Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering, anthropic, generative-ai, ai, llms, claude-mythos-fable

hubie writes: Study challenges belief that temple's curves were designed to correct optical illusions that would have ruined its clean lines: A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the longest-running myths in history after studying optical illusions and the Parthenon, the famed Greek temple that overlooks Athens. Scholars have marvelled at the building on the Acropolis hill for more than 2,000 years and heaped praise on its architects for their clever use of geometry. Its subtle curves are said to correct optical illusions that would have otherwise ruined the Parthenon's clean lines. But after a detailed investigation, and a flurry of mathematical modelling, Prof Alain Goriely at the University of Oxford has reached an awkward conclusion. The optical illusions the curves are meant to fix are either nonsense or practically imperceptible. In short, the illusions are themselves an illusion. In his study, Goriely traces the myth back to the 1st-century Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius who wrote about the Parthenon 400 years after its construction.

### Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
Source: Simon Willison's Weblog
Published: 2026-11-09 23:57 UTC
URL: https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/9/mysterious-beeps/
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Updated: 2026-11-09 23:57 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-10 17:25 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Simon Willison's Weblog [computing_cultures] https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/9/mysterious-beeps/

Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

jelizondo writes: Gizmodo has an interesting article about AI suppressing wages: The New York Times published a new article Friday asking whether artificial intelligence tools have caused disruptions in the number of Americans who are employed. Incredibly, the article never mentions the word "wages."The piece, titled "A.I. Was Supposed to Come for Our Jobs. So Far, Evidence Is Mixed," was written by Ben Casselman and starts with the question we all have: Is artificial intelligence taking our jobs? It's arguably the single biggest question facing the labor market right now, all the more so after Tuesday's midterm elections showed widespread public animosity toward A.I. and data centers, in particular. The evidence, though, is far from clear. The article is mostly fine, even if it's filled with way more questions than answers. Nobody knows long-term whether AI will put a significant dent in jobs: Even if A.I. is taking a toll on hiring, it isn't quite clear what that means. Are companies using A.I. to replace workers?

quietus writes: In an immutable operating system the root file system is locked down (read-only) so that apps and users cannot change or break them. Instead of updating individual system files one by one, updates are installed as a single, complete package all at once, meaning that if anything ever goes wrong, the system can instantly roll back to the last safe, working version. These systems are mainly used with zero-touch installation installations (Internet-of-Things) or as container hosts; their rollback capabilities are appreciated when you're infected by malware, root kits and whatever exploitative flotsam-and-jetsam might hit you through the internet. The probably best known examples of immutable systems are Android and Chromebook, while an immutable Linux distro, bazzite, is making waves in the gaming world. In its latest release, Leap 16.1, SuSE Linux lets you choose between a conventional installation, or the installation of its immutable version of the same operating system.

Linus Torvalds has released the 7.4-rc2 prepatch and it will come as no surprise that it is a large one ("a big -rc2 to go with the largest ever -rc1"). Much of the size was made up of some automated Coccinelle updates that were spread out all over the tree; once those are factored out, the rest looks fairly normal: When masking that noise out from the diffstat, the shape of it changes - not spread out over thousands of files any more. But it does not look unusual: a third is drivers (gpu, networking and sound account for most of it, but there's a bit of everything), another third is networking and bpf, and the final third is "the rest" (mostly filesystems, mm, arch updates). And yes, much of this was driven by various AI fixes. I think I'll stop repeating that, and we can just take it for granted. But this time around Alexei [Starovoitov] claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true.

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/bliki/LLM-Voice.html

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”.

Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R5 · P5 · baseline

Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/rachels-ramblings/good-devs-wary.html

TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right.

Andrej Karpathy sees a widening gap in how people see LLM capabilities. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly.

Hello! I’ve been working on a Django site recently, and I decided to use SQLite as the database. When I was getting started with using SQLite as database for a website I read a bunch of blog posts about how it is totally fine to use SQLite in production for a small site and I think it is totally fine, but what I did not fully appreciate is that SQLite is still a database, databases are complicated, and I do not know a lot about operating databases. So here are a couple of small things I’ve been learning about running SQLite. This is the 4th website I’ve used SQLite for, and I think this one is harder because with the power of the Django ORM I’ve been making the database do more work than I was previously without Django. I started by turning on WAL mode like all the blog posts said to do and hoping for the best. ANALYZE is apparently important Today I was running a query (using SQLite’s FTS5 for full-text search) on a table with 4000 rows and it took 5 seconds. That seemed wrong to me: computers are fast! It turned out that what I needed to do was to run ANALYZE!

To answer a complex business question, an AI agent must understand two things: what happened, and why. The what is a governed metric, like revenue at risk; the why is the network of relationships that produced it. Because metric definitions, a.k.a. measures, traditionally live in business intelligence (BI) platforms while relationships live in knowledge graphs, an AI agent only ever sees half the picture. It guesses the rest, leading to confident but sometimes wrong answers. To solve this hallucination problem, we introduced measures in BigQuery, which are now generally available. Historically, organizations needing both BI and knowledge graphs had to run two siloed technology stacks: one to calculate reliable metrics, the other to map out entity relationships. Bridging them entailed brittle data pipelines and runtime reconciliation by analysts and AI agents, who held the connections in their heads or in sprawling prompts.

CodeMender: AI powered vulnerability fixes right in GitHub PRs To help you secure more code, more quickly, we’ve built CodeMender, our autonomous code-security agent that can find and fix software flaws at machine speed. Standard Network Policies limit you to applying policies at the namespace level, but ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP) lets you apply granular networking policies across an entire cluster. When you use CNP, you can easily scale security and governance policies. Recently, I experimented with this functionality in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and saw the benefits for myself. In this post, we'll explore using CNP to control traffic to an LLM and cluster. If you want to jump right into a hands-on lab, check out this Codelab: Secure AI Inference Workloads with GKE ClusterNetworkPolicy. How CNP works CNP follows a three-tier flow with a precedence match: Admin tier (top precedence): Cluster administrator enforces mandatory security rules that can't be bypassed (for example, blocking metadata access). Network policy tier (middle precedence): Standard namespace-scoped policies that are managed by application teams to control ingress and egress for their microservices.

Speed Insights and Web Analytics now fully support custom environments. Previously, data captured on deployments to a custom environment was attributed to the Preview environment. That data is now attributed to the custom environment it came from, so you can track performance and traffic for staging, QA, or canary environments separately from Production and Preview. You can view this data in several places: Dashboard: use the Environment dropdown in Speed Insights and Web Analytics to pick a custom environment CLI: query it with the vc metrics command Query builder: filter and break down by environment Aggregation API: query it programmatically (Web Analytics only) This change only affects how data is attributed. No new data points are collected, and no configuration changes are needed. Custom environments are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Learn more in the environments documentation. Read more
